strengths: Novel hierarchical identity-preserving attention mechanism (intra-subject, inter-subject, cross-modal) that is well-motivated as an alternative to naive token concatenation used by prior work such as Phantom and Concat-ID.
Integration of a pretrained VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) as a semantically richer conditioning encoder than standard text encoders, with an ablation confirming its contribution to text-video alignment.

First application (to the authors' knowledge) of online RL (Flow-GRPO with a composite quality/identity reward) to the multi-subject subject-consistent video generation setting, addressing known limitations of standard diffusion losses in aligning fine-grained identity concepts.

Extensive quantitative comparison against many open-source (Phantom, SkyReels-A2, VACE) and proprietary (Vidu, Pika, Kling) baselines, with consistent improvements across FaceSim, GmeScore, NexusScore, and NaturalScore.
Thorough ablation studies (hierarchical attention, VLM encoder, curated data) with both quantitative (Table 2) and qualitative (Figure 5) evidence isolating each component's contribution.

A new large-scale, carefully curated multi-source dataset (OpenS2V-Nexus-based, synthetic, and professionally shot video) with documented statistics and a comparison of reference-image construction strategies (data augmentation vs. Flux-Kontext vs. GPT-4o vs. their Gemini-based pipeline), which could be a useful community resource if released as promised.
Demonstrated downstream applicability to zero-shot controllable video editing (subject replacement, background modification), broadening potential impact beyond the core generation task.
weaknesses: Section B.2 'Details of Reward Calculation,' which should specify how R_qual and R_id are computed and how reward hacking is mitigated (a claim made in the related work), is essentially empty in the manuscript as provided, leaving a core novel component (the RL reward design) underspecified and hindering reproducibility.
No quantitative ablation isolates the online RL stage's contribution; only qualitative examples (Figure 5, right panel) are shown, while Table 2 ablates only architecture and data, not RL vs. no-RL.

Evaluation relies entirely on automated/learned metrics (FaceSim, GmeScore, NexusScore, NaturalScore) computed with the authors' own or other model-based scorers; no human/user study is reported to validate perceptual quality, identity preservation, or prompt alignment claims, despite such claims being central to the paper.

Evaluation set size (180 unique subject-text pairs from a single benchmark, OpenS2V-Nexus) is relatively narrow for establishing generalization across the wide range of scenarios (objects, environments, nature) the dataset claims to cover; no variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported.

No analysis of computational cost, inference latency, or parameter count trade-offs relative to baselines, despite the model integrating a 7B VLM plus a 14B DiT backbone—an important practical consideration acknowledged only briefly as a limitation without supporting numbers.

The data curation pipeline depends on proprietary tools (Gemini-Flash-Image, Qwen2.5-VL, Grounding DINO, SAM) for subject decomposition and captioning; while code/data release is promised, reliance on closed-source generative components for the training data itself raises reproducibility and long-term availability concerns.
Minor inconsistencies in metric naming between Table 1 ('GmeScore') and Table 2 ('Text-Video Align.') could confuse readers about whether these are the same metric.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: open-domain multi-subject video generation conditioned on text and multiple reference images, with clear practical applications (personalized content, virtual storytelling, product placement).

The hierarchical attention design (intra-subject -> inter-subject -> multi-modal) is a reasonable and interpretable architectural choice that plausibly addresses the token-concatenation conflicts noted in prior MMDiT-based subject injection methods.

Reports broad quantitative comparisons against multiple open-source (Phantom, VACE, SkyReels-A2) and proprietary (Vidu, Pika, Kling) baselines across several automated metrics (FaceSim, GmeScore, NexusScore, NaturalScore), and includes qualitative figures and a controllable video-editing application demo.

The data-curation pipeline (VLM-based captioning/subject decomposition plus Gemini-Flash-Image synthesis for diverse reference sets) is a potentially useful contribution to the community if the described dataset and code are actually released, and is documented in reasonable detail in the appendix (Figs. 7-9).
weaknesses: Appendix Section B.2 'Details of Reward Calculation' is essentially empty/missing content (just a heading, no text), despite the RL reward being presented as one of the three core contributions; without this, the online RL / GRPO component is not reproducible and its design (e.g., how R_qual and R_id are computed, weighting, reward-hacking mitigation) cannot be assessed.

Potential train/test contamination concern: the training data curation explicitly uses OpenS2V-Nexus as one of three primary data sources, while the evaluation protocol is also 'following the benchmark protocol of OpenS2V-Nexus' using 180 unique subject-text pairs from the same source; the paper does not clarify disjointness between training and evaluation subsets, which undermines the validity of the reported state-of-the-art numbers.

No quantitative ablation isolating the effect of the online RL stage on the main benchmark metrics -- only a qualitative figure (Fig. 5, right panel) is shown; Table 2 ablations cover hierarchical attention, VLM encoder, and curated data, but not the RL phase that is advertised as a key contribution in the abstract and introduction.

The method does not uniformly outperform baselines: e.g., the Aesthetics metric for Ours-14B is lower than several baselines (VACE-1.3B/14B, Phantom-1.3B/14B), and this trade-off (heavier identity-preservation apparatus vs. perceptual quality) is not discussed or analyzed in the text.

Novelty is incremental: the hierarchical local-global attention structure is explicitly inspired by prior work (Wang et al. 2025a; Lin et al. 2025), and using a pretrained VLM as a text/visual encoder and applying Flow-GRPO (an existing method) to this setting are largely engineering combinations of existing components rather than fundamentally new techniques.

No human preference study or user evaluation is reported; all quantitative claims rely on automated/model-based metrics (several of which are themselves VLM/CLIP-based judgments), which is a weaker form of evidence for subjective qualities like identity preservation and naturalness, especially given the RLVR training explicitly optimizes against similar learned reward signals, raising reward-hacking/metric-gaming concerns that the paper only mentions in passing without concrete mitigation evidence.

Reproducibility is currently limited: code, trained models, and the curated dataset are all stated as 'will be released' rather than being available, and several implementation details (e.g., exact reward model architectures, RL hyperparameters, training schedule for the RL phase) are absent from both the main text and appendix.

The system is computationally heavy (14B DiT backbone plus a 7B VLM encoder), and while this is acknowledged under limitations, no efficiency/latency comparison against baselines is provided despite the architectural overhead being substantial relative to prior single-encoder approaches.

strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated and practically relevant problem (multi-subject video generation with identity preservation), which is underexplored compared to single-subject subject-to-video methods.

The hierarchical identity-preserving attention (intra-subject, inter-subject, multi-modal) is a sensible architectural design that explicitly separates concerns which prior concatenation-based approaches (Phantom, Concat-ID, etc.) conflate.

Replacing the standard text encoder with a VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) to jointly encode text and reference images is a reasonable way to inject richer cross-modal semantic guidance, and the ablation (Table 2) shows a clear benefit for text-video alignment.

The paper contributes a large, carefully curated multi-source dataset (OpenS2V-derived, synthetically edited, and high-fidelity licensed videos) with a documented curation pipeline (VLM captioning/subject decomposition, Grounding DINO/SAM masking, Gemini-Flash-Image subject synthesis), and compares this pipeline favorably against naive augmentation, Flux-Kontext, and GPT-4o alternatives in the appendix.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental section: quantitative comparison against multiple open-source (Phantom, VACE, SkyReels-A2) and proprietary (Vidu, Pika, Kling) baselines at two model scales (1.3B/14B), plus ablations isolating each proposed component and a qualitative controllable-editing application.
The writing and figures are generally clear, and the overall pipeline (Fig. 2) is easy to follow.
weaknesses: Appendix B.2 'Details of Reward Calculation' is an empty heading with no content, despite the paper explicitly claiming this appendix provides reproducibility details; the concrete formulations of R_qual and R_id (which models/losses compute them, how they are combined, and how reward hacking is mitigated) are never specified anywhere in the paper, which is a significant gap given RL is advertised as a key contribution.

The claim in Sec 4.2 that ID-Composer 'outperform[s] existing open-source models by a significant margin' across 'all evaluation metrics' is not fully supported by Table 1: e.g., VACE-1.3B (48.24%) and Pika2.1 (46.87%) exceed Ours-14B's Aesthetics score (45.00%), and Kling1.6's Motion score (41.60%) exceeds Ours-14B's (40.00%). This overstatement should be corrected or qualified.

Evaluation relies entirely on automated metrics (FaceSim, GmeScore, NexusScore, NaturalScore), several of which are themselves computed using VLM/MLLM backbones (e.g., GmeScore uses Qwen2-VL, NaturalScore uses an MLLM) that are architecturally similar to the components the proposed method itself uses (Qwen2.5-VL encoder). This raises a risk of evaluation bias favoring VLM-integrated methods, and no human/user study is included to corroborate identity-preservation or quality claims.

Because the RL reward is not fully specified, it is unclear whether the training reward correlates with (or partially reuses concepts from) the reported evaluation metrics (FaceSim/identity, quality), which would make the reported gains partly circular rather than purely indicative of generalizable improvement.

No quantitative ablation isolates the contribution of the online RL (GRPO) stage; Table 2 only ablates hierarchical attention, VLM encoder, and curated data, while the RL stage's benefit is shown only qualitatively (Fig. 5, right panel) on a single example (Einstein), which is weak evidence for a claimed core contribution.

The additional VLM text/image encoder (7B parameters) and RL post-training substantially increase model size and training cost relative to baselines (e.g., Phantom, SkyReels-A2), but the paper does not report compute/parameter-adjusted comparisons, making it hard to judge whether gains stem from the proposed mechanisms or simply from a much larger conditioning encoder.

FaceSim, the primary identity metric emphasized in the results, is inherently face-specific and may not adequately capture identity/appearance preservation for non-human object subjects (e.g., sneakers, cameras, phones) that are highlighted as a use case in Fig. 1 and Fig. 4.
Code, models, and the curated dataset are only promised for future release and are not available with the submission, limiting present-day reproducibility verification.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated hierarchical identity-preserving attention (intra-subject, inter-subject, cross-modal) that is ablated stage-by-stage, showing consistent, interpretable gains in FaceSim/NexusScore.

First application (to the authors' knowledge) of online RL (GRPO/Flow-GRPO) with a composite, task-specific reward (fidelity + quality, including a NaturalScore term to counter reward hacking) to multi-subject video diffusion; ablations on reward components and comparison to offline DPO support the design choices.

Integrates a pretrained VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) as a semantic/cross-modal grounding module rather than a conventional text encoder, with an ablation showing measurable alignment gains over a single T5 encoder.

Constructs and will release a large-scale curated multi-subject video dataset via a non-trivial VLM + image-editing pipeline, with reasonable statistics and comparison against alternative reference-construction strategies (data augmentation, Flux-Kontext, GPT-4o).

Reasonably broad empirical validation: quantitative comparison to multiple open-source and proprietary baselines, qualitative comparisons, an ablation table, and a human preference study (200 questionnaires, 30 participants) that corroborates automated metrics and partially addresses circularity/reward-hacking concerns.
Demonstrates a useful downstream application (zero-shot subject-consistent video editing) beyond the core generation task.
weaknesses: Several evaluation metrics used for both training reward and testing (NexusScore, NaturalScore) are derived from the authors' own benchmark/pipeline, raising concern about circularity/self-serving evaluation despite the human study; the human study itself only compares against 4 baselines with a modest participant pool.

The 14B 'large-scale' model underperforms the smaller 1.3B RL-tuned model on several key metrics (e.g., FaceSim 60.71% vs 66.10%) in Table 1, and this counter-intuitive scaling result is not explained or discussed in the text.
A broken cross-reference ('Tab. ??') in Section 4.3 indicates incomplete proofreading/compilation, a minor but non-trivial presentation flaw.

The ethics statement claims the dataset avoids real-world public figures, yet Figures 1 and 4 explicitly show generation with recognizable public figures (e.g., Albert Einstein, apparent Taylor Swift reference in Fig. 2's example prompt), which is inconsistent with the stated mitigation and raises a minor ethical/representational concern.

The core technical contribution is largely a careful integration of existing techniques (Flow-GRPO/GRPO, VLM encoders, hierarchical cross-attention, DreamBooth-style curation) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; novelty is more in combination/application than in algorithmic invention.

Evaluation set size (180 subject-text pairs) is relatively small for claims of general robustness across 'complex, real-world scenarios', and there is no analysis of failure cases, limits on number of subjects, or robustness beyond the examples shown.

Code/model/dataset release is stated as future ('will be released'), so reproducibility cannot be independently verified from the manuscript alone; several hyperparameters (e.g., reward weight choices) appear empirically set without deeper justification of sensitivity beyond one ablation table.

strengths: The hierarchical identity-preserving attention (intra-subject, inter-subject, cross-modal) is a reasonably motivated architectural design, and Table S.5 provides a clean per-stage ablation showing each stage contributes incrementally.

Integrating a VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) as a semantic grounding module into a DiT video backbone, rather than a conventional text encoder, is a sensible idea for handling complex multi-subject prompts, and the ablation removing the VLM encoder supports its utility.

The paper attempts a fairly broad empirical evaluation, comparing against several open-source (VACE, Phantom, SkyReels-A2) and proprietary (Vidu, Pika, Kling) baselines, and includes both 1.3B and 14B model variants.
Inclusion of a human preference study (Fig. S.13) is a good practice to partially validate automated metrics and address potential reward-hacking concerns.

The data curation pipeline (combining OpenS2V-Nexus, high-fidelity internal videos, and synthetic cross-subject compositions via image editing models) is described in reasonable detail and targets a genuine data scarcity problem for multi-subject video generation.
weaknesses: Strong circularity/validity concern: the RL reward functions (FaceSim/ArcFace, NexusScore, NaturalScore, Q-Align) are nearly identical to, or directly derived from, the evaluation metrics (FaceSim, NexusScore, NaturalScore) used in Table 1/2/3 to claim state-of-the-art performance. Optimizing directly against the test metrics via RL and then reporting large gains on those same metrics substantially weakens the evidentiary value of the quantitative comparison; the human study (200 judgments from 30 participants) is too small and under-specified (no details on blinding, video selection, or statistical significance) to fully offset this.

The manuscript contains an unresolved LaTeX cross-reference error ("As shown in Tab. ??" on page 8), indicating insufficient proofreading before submission; combined with multiple other typos (e.g., "determinsitic", lowercase sentence starts), this reduces confidence in the overall rigor of the writing and preparation.

Ethics statement claims the dataset curation and generations avoid "real-world public figures," yet the qualitative figures and teaser (Fig. 1, Fig. 4) prominently use recognizable figures (e.g., Albert Einstein) and the architecture figure's example prompt explicitly names "Taylor Swift" — a direct contradiction that is not addressed.

Core comparisons rely on self-constructed/derived benchmarks (NexusScore, GmeScore, NaturalScore, built on the authors' own OpenS2V-Nexus-based pipeline) rather than independent, widely validated metrics, and no variance/error bars or statistical testing are reported for any of the reported percentage gains across Tables 1–3, making it hard to assess whether improvements are meaningful or within noise.

Novelty claims are somewhat overstated: the paper claims to "pioneer" online RL for multi-subject video generation, but GRPO-style online RL for video/human-identity generation is already explored in cited concurrent works (e.g., Identity-GRPO, DanceGRPO, Flow-GRPO), making the contribution more incremental (task-specific reward design) than foundational.

The data curation pipeline depends on closed, proprietary commercial models (e.g., "Nano Banana"/Gemini image editing, GPT-4o for comparison) for generating training data, which raises reproducibility concerns: future researchers without access to these exact proprietary APIs may not be able to reconstruct the curated dataset even if it is eventually released.

The "contrastive learning mechanism" mentioned in the introduction as mitigating reward hacking is never formally defined or detailed in the Method section (Sec. 3.3) or appendix, leaving a described component of the system underspecified and unverifiable.

Ablation studies (Table 2, Table S.5, Table S.7) are conducted only on the 1.3B base model; the 14B "large-scale" variant that achieves the headline best numbers in Table 1 is not subjected to any ablation or analysis, leaving open whether the architectural claims generalize to the larger, actually best-performing model.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored and practically important problem: identity-preserving generation for MULTIPLE subjects in video, where prior single-subject methods and naive multi-subject extensions suffer from identity leakage/conflict.

The hierarchical identity-preserving attention (intra-subject -> gated inter-subject -> cross-modal) is a sensible, well-motivated architectural design, and the ablation in Table 2 / Table S.5 shows each stage contributes measurably to FaceSim/NexusScore.

Integrating a pretrained VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) as the semantic conditioning backbone instead of a conventional text encoder is a reasonable and empirically supported design choice (ablation shows large drop in text-video alignment when replaced by T5).

First application (to the authors' knowledge) of online GRPO-style RL with a composite, task-specific reward to multi-subject video diffusion, with a group-relative advantage formulation that avoids training a separate value network; ablation against offline DPO and an SFT baseline (Table 3) shows consistent gains.

Substantial, carefully engineered data curation pipeline (OpenS2V-Nexus + VLM captioning + image-editing-based subject synthesis + curated high-fidelity clips) explicitly designed to mitigate 'copy-paste' artifacts and generalize cross-subject composition, with an ablation demonstrating its necessity.

Broad empirical evaluation: comparisons against multiple open-source (VACE, Phantom, SkyReels-A2) and proprietary (Vidu, Pika, Kling) baselines, plus qualitative comparisons, a reward-hacking-aware human preference study (200 questionnaires, 30 participants), and a fairly extensive appendix with hyperparameters, architecture specs, and additional ablations (fidelity-reward balance, hierarchical-attention stage removal), aiding reproducibility.
Demonstrated zero-shot downstream applicability (controllable video editing: subject insertion/replacement) beyond the core generation task.
weaknesses: Potential reward-metric circularity: two of the three evaluation metrics reported as SOTA gains (NexusScore, NaturalScore) are the authors' own proposed benchmark metrics that are also directly used as RL reward signals (R_fid uses NexusScore-derived subject score, R_qual uses NaturalScore). This raises concern that the large reported gains partly reflect direct optimization of the evaluation metrics themselves rather than independent quality improvements; the human study only partially alleviates this since the specific model variant, statistical significance, and evaluation protocol for that study are not fully specified.

Table 1 mixes parameter scales in a way that makes 'SOTA' claims for the smaller 1.3B model inconsistent (e.g., Phantom-14B still exceeds Ours-1.3B on Aesthetics), and the headline 14B model's improvements over some proprietary systems (e.g., Aesthetics vs. Kling 1.6, Motion vs. Kling 1.6) are marginal or mixed rather than uniformly dominant, despite the abstract's claim of 'new state-of-the-art performance... across all evaluation metrics.'
A broken internal cross-reference ('As shown in Tab. ??') in Section 4.3/related RL analysis indicates incomplete proofreading, suggesting other unchecked details may exist.

Computational cost of the online RL stage is only qualitatively discussed (Appendix E.1) without quantified wall-clock/GPU-hour overhead, despite RL on a video diffusion policy with VLM-based reward computation and multi-step SDE rollouts being potentially very expensive; this limits reproducibility and practical assessment of the method's cost-effectiveness.
The 'Total Score' aggregation in Table 1 (normalized weighted sum of heterogeneous metrics with different scales/ranges) is not clearly specified, making the headline ranking somewhat opaque.

Evaluation is restricted to 480p resolution and a single base architecture (Wan-Video 1.3B/14B); generalizability of the hierarchical attention + VLM + RL recipe to other video DiT backbones or higher resolutions is untested.

Originality claims relative to closely related prior work (e.g., CINEMA, Concat-ID, which are noted as also using attention/VLM-style guidance) could be more precisely delineated; the paper asserts novelty ('no prior open-source work has integrated a VLM as the core reasoning engine') without a detailed side-by-side comparison of design differences from these related methods.
